note_tweet.text: When running RL with prior data, a behavior constraint is important to trade off exploration vs staying close to known good parts of the data. But the choice of this constraint is delicate -- we don't want to just match all the prior data, but we don't want to wander too far. In our new paper, we propose a new constraint that combines support constraints with continuous penalties to enable excellent offline to online RL performance.

note_tweet.text:
One of the biggest data bottlenecks in robotics is turning raw human video into high-quality training labels.

Perceptron Egocentric 1.0 is a self-service API that turns first-person human and robot video into structured training data:

- Timestamped subtask timelines, down to sub-second actions
- A separate activity timeline for each hand (or gripper)
- State-of-the-art 3D hand reconstruction, no camera calibration needed

It claims to match GPT-6 Astra on subtask quality at ~1/8 the cost ($9 vs ~$76 per video-hour), full stack at $29.

The pipes to leverage the cheapest robot training data just got more viable.

note_tweet.text:
An AI model that helps transfer human motion, recorded with LiberSense Glove, into robot skills.

That’s LiberAI’s Liber-0: a World Action Model pretrained on 2.2M+ hours of human experience.

The headline result: 36% overall success across 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks and 600 trials, without training on robot demos collected specifically for those tasks.

Another proof point stood out: across eight tasks, 25% of the robot-demo pool plus the full glove pool achieved a progress score of 75.6, versus 72.8 with the full robot pool alone. The full pools contained equal numbers of demos.

Fewer robot demos, supplemented by human demonstrations, and stronger observed performance.

If human experience transfers this efficiently at greater scale, the data wall in robotics could start to crack.
@liberai_robo

note_tweet.text:
Exclusive: Everyone is racing toward AGI and general-purpose robots. @xiao_ted has been thinking deeply about the problem almost nobody is naming: even if both arrive, what still limits progress in the physical world?

Ted argues it comes down to verification, how long it takes to trust an answer. In sim, a humanoid learns to walk in 15 minutes. In the real world, checking a single robot policy can take 100+ hours. Progress moves at the speed of verification, not intelligence.

A genuinely different way to see the field.
https://t.co/3TiwdubePi
